title: Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums
directAnswer: Both arrays are sorted ascending. The smallest possible sum is nums1[0]+nums2[0]. Seed a min-heap with the pairs (nums1[i], nums2[0]) for the first min(k, len(nums1)) rows, keyed by sum. Pop the smallest each time — that pair is the next answer — and push its right neighbour (i, j+1) in the same row. This expands only the frontier of candidates, giving O(k log k) instead of materialising all m·n sums.

remember.pattern: Min-heap over a sorted grid frontier (k-way merge)
remember.formula:
heap = [(nums1[i] + nums2[0], i, 0) for i in range(min(k, len(nums1)))]
repeat k times:
    (s, i, j) = heap.pop_min()
    emit (nums1[i], nums2[j])
    if j + 1 < len(nums2): heap.push((nums1[i] + nums2[j+1], i, j+1))
rules: **Seed one entry per row**, not the whole grid — start each row at its smallest column j=0.
On popping `(i, j)`, push only `(i, j+1)` — the next-smallest in *that* row; never push `(i+1, j)` (its row was already seeded).
Cap the seed at **min(k, len(nums1))** rows — you can never need more than k starting points.
Store **(sum, i, j)** in the heap so it orders by sum and you can reconstruct both values and find the neighbour.
Think of it as **merging len(nums1) sorted lists** (each row is sorted because nums2 is sorted) and taking the k smallest heads.
Guard empty inputs and `k == 0` up front — return an empty list.

remember.takeaway: When two sorted arrays form a monotone sum grid, the k smallest sums live on an expanding frontier you can explore with a min-heap — exactly the k-way merge trick. Seed the cheapest cell of each row, and every pop reveals the next answer while pushing just its successor. The same frontier idea solves Kth Smallest in a Sorted Matrix and merging k sorted lists.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you exploit the sorted structure to avoid generating all m·n sums, and whether you see the problem as a k-way merge driven by a min-heap on an expanding frontier.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Generating every pair and sorting (O(m·n log(m·n)) time and space), or pushing both (i+1,j) and (i,j+1) on each pop — which double-counts pairs and explodes the heap.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Call it a k-way merge: 'each row i is the sorted list nums1[i]+nums2[*]; I'm merging len(nums1) sorted lists and taking k heads.' Then justify pushing only the right neighbour to avoid duplicates.

problemStatement:
You are given two integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2` sorted in **non-decreasing order** and an integer `k`.

Define a pair `(u, v)` which consists of one element from the first array and one element from the second array.

Return *the* `k` *pairs* `(u₁, v₁), (u₂, v₂), ..., (uₖ, vₖ)` *with the smallest sums*.
constraints: nums1 and nums2 both sorted in non-decreasing order
understanding: Both arrays are sorted. A 'pair' takes one value from each array; its cost is the sum. Return the k pairs (as value pairs, not indices) with the smallest sums. There may be fewer than k total pairs if the arrays are tiny — return all of them in that case.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the input arrays guaranteed sorted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, non-decreasing. That's the whole point — it lets the heap explore a monotone frontier instead of all m·n sums.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I return indices or the actual value pairs?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Value pairs, e.g. [nums1[i], nums2[j]]. Unlike Two Sum, this asks for the values.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can there be fewer than k pairs total?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, if len(nums1)·len(nums2) < k. The heap naturally drains and you return whatever you collected.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can values be negative or duplicated?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes to both. Sums can be negative; duplicates produce legitimately repeated pairs. The sum-ordering still holds.

examples.explanation: Smallest sums are 1+2=3, 1+4=5, 1+6=7. Row i=0 (value 1) dominates because 1 is far smaller than 7 or 11.
Both 1s in nums1 pair with the 1 in nums2 for sum 2. Duplicates are valid distinct pairs (different source indices).
Only 2 pairs exist (2×1 grid) though k=3 — return all of them.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Generate All Pairs and Sort
approaches.whenToMention: State it first to establish correctness and the m·n cost you're about to beat using sortedness.
hints: There are len(nums1) × len(nums2) possible pairs. What's the most direct way to find the k with the smallest sums?
Form every pair, sort all of them by sum, and take the first k.
This ignores that the arrays are sorted — note that as the inefficiency you'll fix next.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building all m·n pairs is O(m·n); sorting them is O(m·n log(m·n)); both arrays up to 10⁵ make m·n up to 10¹⁰ pairs — infeasible in time and memory. But it's obviously correct.
approaches.explanation:
The most literal reading: a pair is any `(nums1[i], nums2[j])`, there are `m·n` of them, so generate them all, sort by sum, and slice the first `k`.

**Why it's correct.** It enumerates the entire universe of pairs, so the k smallest sums are guaranteed to be in the sorted prefix. There is no cleverness to get wrong.

**Why it throws away the gift.** The problem hands us two *sorted* arrays and we ignore that entirely. Sorting `m·n` items when we only want `k` of them (and `k` ≤ 10⁴ ≪ m·n ≤ 10¹⁰) is enormously wasteful — we sort 10 billion sums to read off the first ten thousand.

**Why we don't ship this.** Beyond being slow, it's a *memory* bomb: storing `m·n` pairs blows the heap for large inputs. The fix is to never materialise pairs we don't need. Sortedness means the cheapest sums cluster in the top-left of the conceptual sum grid, and we can walk outward from there with a min-heap — the optimal approach.

**When it's still acceptable.** If both arrays are tiny (so `m·n` is small) or `k` is close to `m·n`, generate-and-sort is simpler and competitive. Mention that nuance; interviewers like calibrated answers.
approaches.insight: Generating all pairs ignores that the smallest sums are concentrated near nums1[0]+nums2[0] because both arrays are sorted. Recognising that 'cheap sums live in the top-left corner of the grid' is the bridge to the heap solution.

code.python:
def kSmallestPairs(self, nums1: list[int], nums2: list[int], k: int) -> list[list[int]]:
    all_pairs = [[x, y] for x in nums1 for y in nums2]
    all_pairs.sort(key=lambda p: p[0] + p[1])
    return all_pairs[:k]

approaches.name: Min-Heap over the Sorted Frontier (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as a k-way merge of len(nums1) sorted rows.
hints: Picture an m×n grid where cell (i,j) holds nums1[i]+nums2[j]. Because both arrays are sorted, sums increase going right and going down. Where is the smallest sum?
The smallest is the top-left (0,0). The next smallest must be a neighbour of cells already chosen — explore a frontier with a min-heap keyed by sum.

Seed the heap with column 0 of each row: (nums1[i]+nums2[0], i, 0). Pop the min, record the pair, and push (i, j+1). Repeat k times. Pushing only the right neighbour avoids duplicates because each row was seeded exactly once.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The heap holds at most min(k, m) seeds plus one push per pop, so its size stays O(k). We do k pop+push cycles, each O(log k) → O(k log k) time, O(k) space. Independent of the (huge) m·n.
approaches.explanation:
Model the sums as an `m × n` grid: cell `(i, j)` is `nums1[i] + nums2[j]`. Because both arrays are sorted non-decreasingly, sums increase as you move **right** (larger `nums2[j]`) and as you move **down** (larger `nums1[i]`). The grid is monotone in both directions, so the cheapest sums hug the top-left corner.

**Why seed one cell per row.** Each row `i` is itself a sorted list: `nums1[i]+nums2[0] ≤ nums1[i]+nums2[1] ≤ …`. The whole problem is therefore a **k-way merge** of `min(k, m)` sorted lists, and the classic way to merge sorted lists is a min-heap seeded with each list's head. The head of row `i` is its column-0 cell `(nums1[i]+nums2[0], i, 0)`. We only need `min(k, m)` rows because we'll emit at most `k` pairs and each emitted pair frees at most one new candidate.

**Why we push only `(i, j+1)`, never `(i+1, j)`.** This is the subtle correctness point. When we pop cell `(i, j)`, the only *new* candidate it unlocks is its right neighbour `(i, j+1)` — the next-cheapest sum in the *same* row. We must **not** also push the down-neighbour `(i+1, j)`, because row `i+1` was already given its own seed at `(i+1, 0)` and will advance through its own columns independently. If we pushed both directions, cell `(i+1, j)` would be reachable from two paths — from `(i, j)` going down and from `(i+1, j-1)` going right — and we'd insert it twice, double-counting pairs and bloating the heap. Seeding rows once + advancing only rightward guarantees each cell enters the heap **exactly once**.

**Why this is correct (the frontier argument).** At any moment the heap contains the cheapest not-yet-emitted cell of every row that has been 'opened'. The global minimum among all un-emitted cells is therefore the heap's top — any cheaper cell would have to be the left neighbour of a heap entry, but that left neighbour was already emitted (which is exactly when we pushed the current entry). So popping the heap top always yields the next-smallest sum overall.

**Cost and Python detail.** We perform `k` cycles of pop + (maybe) push, each `O(log(heap size))` and the heap never exceeds `O(k)` — so `O(k log k)`, completely decoupled from the enormous `m·n`. Python's `heapq` is a min-heap and tuples compare lexicographically, so storing `(sum, i, j)` orders by sum automatically (with `i`, `j` as harmless tie-breakers). Java needs an explicit comparator on the sum.
approaches.insight: It's a k-way merge in disguise: each row is a sorted list, and the smallest sums form an expanding frontier from the top-left. Seeding each row once and advancing only rightward keeps every grid cell entering the heap exactly once — that single discipline is what prevents duplicates and keeps it O(k log k).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Pushing both neighbours (duplicates)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Cell (i+1, j) is reachable both from (i, j) going down and from (i+1, j-1) going right. Pushing both directions inserts it twice, double-counting pairs.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:

result.append([nums1[i], nums2[j]])
if j + 1 < len(nums2):  # only the right neighbour; rows are pre-seeded
    heapq.heappush(min_heap, (nums1[i] + nums2[j+1], i, j+1))

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Seeding every row
commonMistakesDetailed.why: With m up to 10⁵ but k only 10⁴, seeding all m rows wastes time and space. You never need more than k starting points.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Storing the sum but losing the indices
commonMistakesDetailed.why: To push the right neighbour you need to know which row i and column j you popped. Storing only the sum makes that impossible.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: heapq.heappush(min_heap, nums1[i] + nums2[0])  # no i, j -- can't advance
